reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction of the conjunctiva and cornea, presenting as small raised nodules (phlyctens) with surrounding hyperaemia
The classic antigenic triggers are staphylococcal antigens (associated with chronic blepharitis) and, historically or in endemic areas, tuberculoprotein
Conjunctival phlyctens near the limbus are often self-limiting, whereas corneal phlyctens cause marked photophobia, tearing, and blepharospasm
Corneal lesions may migrate centrally, dragging a leash of vessels behind them and leaving a triangular scar with its apex toward the centre
Predominantly affects children and young adults and is more common where tuberculosis and malnutrition are prevalent
Recurrent corneal phlyctens can cause thinning, scarring, and vascularisation with lasting visual impairment
Management pairs treatment of the underlying trigger (lid hygiene for staphylococcal disease, evaluation for tuberculosis) with topical corticosteroids to control the hypersensitivity reaction
Because it may signal underlying tuberculosis, systemic evaluation is warranted, particularly in endemic settings
reference.pathophysiology: Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis is a delayed-type hypersensitivity response to microbial antigens, most often staphylococcal proteins associated with chronic blepharitis, and historically tuberculoprotein. Sensitised T lymphocytes react to the antigen at the limbus, cornea, or conjunctiva, producing a localised nodular infiltrate (the phlycten) with surrounding vascular congestion. The overlying epithelium may ulcerate. Corneal phlyctens can advance centrally, drawing a wedge of new vessels and leaving a scar. Repeated episodes cause progressive corneal vascularisation, thinning, and scarring. As the disorder reflects an immune reaction to a remote antigen rather than active local infection, treatment targets both the antigenic source and the hypersensitivity response.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex or herpes zoster keratitis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting limbal or corneal phlyctens and associated vascular leash
Assessment for blepharitis and staphylococcal lid disease
Tuberculosis evaluation (tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, chest imaging) especially in endemic areas or recurrent disease
Fluorescein staining to assess epithelial ulceration over the phlycten
Screening for malnutrition or systemic predisposition in children
Cultures if secondary infection is suspected
redFlags: Central corneal involvement with scarring and visual loss
Features suggesting underlying active tuberculosis requiring systemic investigation
Corneal thinning or ulceration risking perforation
Recurrent disease indicating an uncontrolled antigenic trigger
reference.prognosis: Conjunctival phlyctens are usually self-limiting and resolve without sequelae, whereas recurrent corneal disease can cause scarring, vascularisation, and lasting visual impairment. Controlling the underlying trigger reduces recurrence and preserves vision.
pitfalls: Treating the eye with steroids without addressing the underlying blepharitis or investigating for tuberculosis
Missing an infective keratitis mimicking a phlycten before prescribing steroids
Overlooking central corneal scarring as a cause of reduced vision
Failing to screen for tuberculosis and malnutrition in at-risk children
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
